title: Remote MCP servers and better tool descriptions

opening.headline: When your model calls the wrong tool, you will find the cause in tooltips and learn how to read and fix remote MCP server connection settings.
body: If a user asks to find last month's order history, but your model calls a product search tool rather than an order lookup tool, it's easy to first question model performance. However, the model does not see the tool's code; it only reads the name, description, and input schema. If the description is ambiguous, the model has no basis for distinguishing between tools.

In this lesson, we'll look at what a tool definition consists of and how to read the configuration line-by-line for connecting a remote MCP server to the Messages API. Next, we explain the process of revising the descriptions of two similar tools and the case of diagnosing the composition of a tool that mixes search and inquiry.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of remote MCP servers and tooltips
The cause of incorrect tool calls can be diagnosed as a lack of tool descriptions.
The effectiveness of the explanation improvement plan can be judged.

screens.title: Model calls the wrong tool
screens.lead: First, read the scene below. I read this while thinking about why the model made this call and whether I should be suspicious of the code or the explanation.

visual.alt: A scene with user requests and incorrectly called tool logs placed above and below.
labels: Find my order history from last month
Arguments: query = last month’s order history

paragraphs: A user asked the order tracking app: Find my order history from last month. The app had two tools registered: `search_orders` and `search_products`. However, the model called the product search tool rather than the ordering tool, and the user received the wrong product list.

If you look at the descriptions of the two tools, you can guess why. The names were similar, and the descriptions were just one line: search for orders and search for products, respectively. The model is blind to the internal code of the tool. All the model reads is the name, description, and input schema. A one-line explanation couldn't tell which tool to use and when.

So the question for this class is this. When a call is wrong, should you suspect the code or the explanation? In the screens that follow, consider who the audience for your tooltip is and take a step-by-step look at how you should write the description.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: When a call is incorrect, where should you check first: the code or the tooltip?

screens.outro: First, let's remember who our readers are when writing tooltips.

screens.title: Who is your audience when writing tooltips?
screens.lead: When you write tooltips, who do you think will read them? Switch between the two states below to compare how the same one-line description reads differently to your fellow developers and the model. You don't need to enter an answer.

states.label: When fellow developers read
states.body:
Even if the description is just one line about searching for an order, there will be no major inconvenience to fellow developers. If you open the tool code or look up the team wiki, you can see what input it receives and what it returns. This is why short memo-like explanations become a habit.

However, if the person writing this explanation considers only colleagues as readers, the explanation will only contain information that can be understood among people who already know each other.

states.label: When the model reads
states.body:
The model can't see the code or the wiki, and has no clues to understand the tool other than the description. A single line to search for an order doesn't tell you when to use this tool and when not to use it, whether your input is an order number or a period, and what you get back as a result.

The real audience of a tooltip is the model. The description is an instruction manual given to the model, so you must manually write down the information needed for the model to select a tool and fill out the parameters.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that the reader is a model, let's take a look at what a tool definition consists of.

screens.title: Configuration of the tool definition: name, description, input_schema
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined item in the text below to see a description of how the model uses that item. Please check the items one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration showing how the tool definition JSON becomes a system prompt passed to the model.
labels: The API compiles definitions and creates system prompts with instructions for using the tool.
All the model reads is this text

data.text: A tool definition looks like this: {"name": "orders_search", "description": "find a customer's past order by order number", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"order_no": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["order_no"]}} Here, name follows the rule of allowing only letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens, with a length between 1 and 128 characters. description is a plain text description detailing what the tool does, when it should be used, and how it operates. input_schema defines parameters using a JSON Schema. In the example above, since required specifies "order_no", the model reads that it must not call the tool without an order number. input_examples provides optional examples of how to invoke the tool. The API combines these definitions to create a tool-use instruction document named system prompt, which the model reads exclusively as text.

terms.tip: The name of the tool. Use only English letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens, and can range from 1 to 128 characters. A similar tool can create boundaries by prefixing the name.
The model is the most important clue when choosing a tool. It is plain text that details what it does, when it is used, and how it operates.
Define the parameters that the tool will receive as JSON Schema. The model looks at this schema and populates the call arguments.
This is a list of essential parameters. Parameters not here are interpreted by the model as ok to omit.
This is optional. By showing an example call, we help the model format its arguments more accurately.
Text that the API gathers tool definitions from and tells the model how to use the tool. This is all the model knows about the tool.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the configuration of the definition, let's read the connection settings when the tool comes from an external server.

screens.title: Remote MCP Server and MCP Connector: Read settings line by line
screens.lead: The MCP Connector is a feature that connects to a remote MCP server from the Messages API without a separate MCP client. Read the settings below along with the line numbers, and check the symptoms when the lines are misaligned in each description.

notes.note: mcp_servers determines the location of the servers. The url must start with https, and the server must be open via HTTP. Since the local STDIO server cannot be connected directly, if this condition is not met, the connection itself will not be established.

authorization_token is an optional item to only put on servers that require an OAuth token. If this line is missing when the server requests authentication, an authentication failure symptom will appear.
name is the name referring to this server. The mcp_server_name in the toolset below must be exactly the same as this value.
mcp_toolset in tools is a setting that exposes the tools of the above server to the model. There must be exactly one toolset per server.
If mcp_server_name is different from the name of the server, a mismatched configuration error will occur. Since even a single letter difference can occur, this is the line to compare first.

If you set enabled in default_config to false and only tools to be used in configs are turned on to true, you can become a whitelist. On the other hand, if you leave all the tools open and turn off only the dangerous tools to false, it will be in the denied list. For read-only assistants, it is recommended to block the write and delete tools.

screens.outro: Now that you've read Server Connections, let's move on and revise the descriptions of similar tools for the reason that descriptions become more important as the number of tools increases.

screens.title: The process of correcting the descriptions of two similar tools
screens.lead: The instructor revises the explanation of the two similar tools once per step. Select the right arrow to follow the pre-improvement and post-improvement changes to see how call accuracy changes.

visual.alt: A bar plot showing the percentage of correct tool selections increasing with each improvement in the description.
labels: Percentage of correct tool selection (value determined by instructor as an example)

steps.title: Before improvement: One-line description
steps.body: The description of the two tools is `search_orders` searches for orders and `search_products` searches for products. Both end with the same verb, search, and there is no indication as to what is being input. In this state, there is insufficient basis for the model to determine which tool the same request will go to by finding the order history from last month.

steps.title: Improvement 1: Write down the target and scope
steps.body: Write down what and to what extent it is covered. For example, `search_orders` is used to find a customer's past orders by order number or period. Once the input criteria and target are revealed, it becomes easier to associate them with words such as order or last month in the request.

steps.title: Improvement 2: Write down when not to use it
steps.body: It's not just about when to use it, but also when not to use it. Add to the description of `search_orders` that it does not answer questions about product information. When boundaries are drawn on both sides, the model is less likely to hesitate between the two.

steps.title: Improvement 3: Create boundaries by name
steps.body: Add a prefix to the name to reveal the functional area, such as `orders_search`, `products_search`. When there are many tools, the prefix in the name tells the model the area at a glance.

steps.title: Describes return contents and ambiguous parameters
steps.body: Include in the description what the tool returns and what ambiguous parameters mean. For example, if you do not specify whether `period` is daily or monthly, the model will guess and fill it in.

steps.title: Repeat improvement through evaluation
steps.body: Descriptions are not written once and done. Iteratively improve your description by evaluating the number of calls, errors, and token usage. The end of this process is to check with indicators whether the rate of selecting the correct tool has increased after improvement.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the improvement process, let us explain an example of diagnosing the composition of a tool that mixes search and inquiry.

screens.title: Case commentary: Constructing a tool that mixes search and inquiry
screens.lead: The instructor will step-by-step diagnose and organize tool configurations with overlapping names and descriptions. Select the right arrow to follow the diagnostic steps.

steps.title: Configuration in question
steps.body: There are four tools listed: Search, Lookup, Find, and Get. The names are all similar, and the explanation is that they all import data. No matter what the user asks, the model can choose any of the four tools, resulting in a jumble of calls.

steps.title: Step 1: Collect call logs
steps.body: First, collect call logs to see which request went to which tool. If you see requests of the same kind scattered across different tools, it's a sign that your tooltips are not distinct.

steps.title: Step 2: Merge or split overlapping tools
steps.body: First, see if tools with overlapping functions can be combined into one. If they cannot be combined, divide the border by name, such as `orders_search`, `orders_get`. Simply reducing the number of tools reduces the choice of models and makes calls more stable.

steps.title: Step 3: Write input criteria and output in the description
steps.body: Write down the input criteria and output content in the description. For example, search is used to find multiple lists using a keyword, and inquiry is used to retrieve details of a single item using an order number. The description should reveal the criteria: lookup if there is a number, or search if there is only a keyword.

steps.title: Step 4: Make the same request again
steps.body: After making the correction, we rerun the original incorrect request to ensure that the call goes to the correct tool. We don't stop with just one hit, we also check with several similar requests.

steps.title: Before blaming the model
steps.body: If I get a call error, I read the explanation first before concluding that the model is deficient. Even if a person reads it, if they don't know the difference between the two tools, they won't know the model either.

screens.outro: This time, we will fix cases where the MCP settings themselves, rather than the explanation, are incorrect.

screens.title: Case commentary: Reading and correcting incorrect MCP settings, and judging the effect of improvement
screens.lead: The instructor corrects problematic MCP settings line by line and finally judges the effectiveness of the improvement. Select the right arrow and follow the steps in order.

steps.title: Problem setting
steps.body: The server definitions are `"url": "http://orders.internal:3000"`, `"name": "orders-mcp"`, and the toolset is `"mcp_server_name": "order-mcp"`. Moreover, even the order cancellation tool is fully open. I assume you have this setting stuck on a read-only order tracking assistant.

steps.title: Step 1: Fix the url
steps.body: The url starts with http and is an internal address. The connector only connects to public servers that start with https. Publishing the server as https is the correct solution, this line is what's causing the connection to stop itself.

steps.title: Step 2: Match the names
steps.body: The name of the server is `orders-mcp`, but the toolset refers to `order-mcp`. Configuration error with mismatched names. Change `mcp_server_name` in the toolset to `orders-mcp` by one letter.

steps.title: Step 3: Block dangerous tools
steps.body: The Cancel Order tool is open in a read-only assistant. Block the tool with `enabled: false` in `configs` in the toolset, or, safer, leave `enabled` in `default_config` to false and turn on only the tools you want to use.

steps.title: Step 4: See the effect with indicators
steps.body: After fixing, we compare the percentage of correct tool selections, number of calls, number of errors, and token usage. If there are many incorrect parameter errors, this is a signal to reinforce the explanation or input examples. If you notice a decrease in the number of calls, it may be a sign to tweak your tool's response range settings.

steps.title: Distinguish between setup errors and explanation errors
steps.body: A connection or name mismatch is a configuration issue, and connecting but calling the wrong tool is an explanation issue. You need to distinguish between symptoms so you can find exactly where to fix it.

screens.outro: Now that I have identified errors in settings and explanations, I will conclude by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: A tooltip is a user manual given to the model. The model only reads the name, description, and input schema, so if a call is incorrect, the description is checked before the code.

A remote MCP server connects with a connector, matches the server's name with the toolset's name, and limits the tools to be used by whitelisting or denylisting them. Similar tools are distinguished by their purpose, when they should not be used, and by name.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the components of the tool definition and MCP connection with their descriptions.
right: Shows an example call as a selection item
Plain text that details what the tool does and when to use it.
checks.explain: description is a key clue for the model to select a tool, input_schema contains the input format, and mcp_servers contains remote server connection information. input_examples is optional.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
Read the following settings to determine the cause of your connection problem.
"mcp_servers": [{"type": "url", "url": "https://orders.example.com/sse", "name": "orders-mcp"}]
"tools": [{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "order-mcp"}]
options: This line is the cause because the url starts with https
The toolset's mcp_server_name is different from the server name (orders-mcp), so they do not match.
If the type is URL, it is treated as a STDIO server and blocked.
If there is no authorization_token, this setting will always be invalid.
checks.explain: The mcp_server_name of the toolset must be the same as the name defined in mcp_servers. The above settings are different for orders-mcp and order-mcp, resulting in a configuration error.

wrong.0: URLs starting with https meet the requirements.
wrong.2: type means url and does not mean STDIO. A separate limitation is that you cannot connect directly to a local STDIO server.
wrong.3: The token is an optional item to be inserted only on servers that require OAuth authentication.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

glossary.def: This is a Model Context Protocol server that is open via HTTP and can be accessed from the outside.
Claude's ability to connect directly to remote MCP servers from the Messages API without the need for a separate MCP client.
This is a field that defines the parameters that the tool will receive in JSON Schema.
One method is to turn on only the tools that will be used in the MCP toolset, and the other is to turn off only dangerous tools. Set with default_config and configs.

misconceptions.myth: Tool call errors are model performance issues.
misconceptions.fact: If the description is ambiguous, the model has no basis for distinguishing between tools. If an error occurs, check the name, description, and schema before blaming the model.

misconceptions.myth: The MCP server connects to any server.
misconceptions.fact: Connectors in the Messages API only connect directly to servers exposed over HTTP. The local STDIO server cannot be connected directly, and the url must start with https.

misconceptions.myth: The longer the tool description, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Division, not length, is key. The purpose, when not to use it, input criteria, and return information must be clear so the model can distinguish between tools.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The tool description is a user manual given to the model.
The remote MCP server connects with a connector, matches the server name and toolset name, and restricts the tools to be used to the allow or deny list.
Similar tools are demarcated by name and description.
The effectiveness of explanation improvement is judged by the percentage of correct tool selection and error indicators.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If I read the two tooltips I wrote with the eyes of a model, would they be distinguishable from each other?
